somat · Nov 18, 2026

The strategic commander always felt like it should have been more successful. On paper it is the perfect the missing half for the native PC FPS controller.

So, the mouse, If you had asked anyone to design a bespoke FPS controller, they would not design a mouse, yet somehow, this thing built to do something totally different, point at things on the screen, has proven to be the best fps controller, nobody has come up with anything better. Probably something about it's huge(for controller sizes) swing distance and absolute positioning.

The problem is the other half, the keyboard, on the one hand it is sort of nice to have 100+ buttons to use, but you almost never need that many and it stinks to only have binary(on/off) movement.

I have seen half controllers designed to solve this, but they never have enough buttons and are hard to hold, but the strategic commander, that makes one think, forget what it was built for, the RTS, it looks awkward as hell for that, but it does look perfect for the FPS.

orbital-decay · Nov 21, 2026

Biomechanically and due to how the nervous system works, the fastest and most precise movements can only be done with full arm movement and fingers for extra accuracy, on a device which is the most reactive (e.g. zero weight/static friction/hysteresis/dead zones) and has a very specific movement resistance (e.g. dynamic friction), low enough but not too low. Many control schemes have been tried over decades but these basic rules seem to give the best results. Which only leaves the scheme most skilled FPS players already prefer: a basic, most lightweight mouse with a properly centered sensor, held with something close to a claw grip, without too many buttons that would mess up your aiming. Plus a keyboard under the other hand, it's a lot less important than the mouse.

Casual FPS play is more forgiving, e.g. gyro seems to work for many people as well (full arm + precise movement again, but not ideally reactive/resistant). But you can't put too many buttons on such a controller either.

MomsAVoxell · Nov 21, 2026

I once wrote an entire book about the Logitech Cyberman joystick/mouse combination and what could be done with it - I was contacted by O'Reilly themselves, because I had one, they'd seen my writing previously, and were convinced that this was going to be the hot new thing for controllers/peripherals, setting a new standard for PC devices ..

https://www.computinghistory.org.uk/det/12416/logitech-cyber...

It seemed like a good idea at the time, but it flopped.

And it was during the course of this project that I discovered why: it was painful to use for longer than 10 or 15 minutes.

So many of these projects start out as a kind of sci-fi fever dream, an ideation of the kinds of control surfaces one would find in space, zooming around asteroids, and .. that is inspiring and beautiful to all of us nerds, I would wager .. except it doesn't take into account the one very, very important element in all control surfaces, which overrides the aesthetic sensibilities and BOM desires of designers and accountants alike: gravity.

Sure, the Cyberman would be awesome in a low-/no-gravity environment, and I'd use it all day/night/epoch as appropriate for getting the cargo docked and transferred to other star systems, mmmkay... but here on Earth the thing is a positive drag and what should've been a few days of serious computing and pixel shredding turns into a forearm torture par excellence.

This is why the very boring, plain old mouse and keyboard have persisted, imho, because they harvest the one bit of energy that is accessible and inescapable on every single desk, for every single type of user in existence: gravity. That flat plane is inescapable. Devices which force you to resist it, even at the digit level, are going to be asking their users to simply do too much work, and the thing will eventually end up in its final destination: the back of some dusty drawer, somewhere ...
